title: Real-Time Chat System: Complete Architecture
description: Design a distributed real-time chat architecture supporting 50M concurrent WebSocket connections, 1:1 and group chats, presence, and Cassandra message history.

data.text: Design a highly scalable, real-time distributed chat system supporting 100+ million daily active users and 50 million concurrent persistent WebSocket connections. The platform facilitates 1-on-1 private messaging, group conversations with thousands of participants, real-time typing indicators, delivery receipts (sent, delivered, read), user presence synchronization, and offline message queueing with sub-100ms delivery latency.

terms.definition: Stateful gateway nodes maintaining persistent TCP/TLS connections to active client devices for bi-directional real-time communication.
A centralized in-memory store (Redis) mapping each `user_id` to their currently active WebSocket Gateway server instance and connection socket ID.
A write-optimized wide-column database ideal for chat history, partitioning messages by `conversation_id` and sorting chronologically by `message_id`.
The 3-stage delivery lifecycle: Server Ack (Message saved), Delivered Receipt (Recipient device confirmed receipt), and Read Receipt (User opened chat).
Clients send a ping every 30-60 seconds; if a ping is missed and the Redis TTL expires, the user is marked offline.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: 1:1 Direct Messaging: Send and receive text messages, emojis, and media attachments with instant delivery
Group Chats: Multi-user conversations up to 5,000 members with participant management and admin roles
Delivery Status Receipts: Real-time visual tracking of Sent, Delivered, and Read states
Presence & Typing Indicators: Display real-time online/offline status and "User is typing..." indicators
Offline Queueing & Sync: Store messages for offline users and synchronize seamlessly upon reconnection
Chat History & Pagination: Infinite scroll chat history with fast backward retrieval by timestamp

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Scale: 50M concurrent WebSocket connections; 10+ billion messages exchanged daily (~115,000 msgs/sec)
Delivery Latency: Sub-100ms end-to-end message delivery between online users
Data Durability: Zero message loss once acknowledged by the server; stored across replicated disk clusters
High Availability: 99.999% uptime for the real-time gateway and message ingestion pipeline
Message Ordering: Strict chronological sequence within any single conversation room

data.text: The architecture isolates stateful WebSocket connection servers from stateless business logic (Auth, User Profiles, Media Uploads). A central Session Registry in Redis routes incoming messages to the specific connection server hosting the recipient's active socket.

data.text: The sequence traces a message from User A to User B. If User B is online, the message arrives over their existing WebSocket connection. If User B is offline, the message is stored in the offline inbox and a push notification is triggered.

data.caption: 1:1 message delivery sequence: Online recipient push via Session Registry vs Offline storage and mobile push notification

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Alice as 👤 Alice (Sender)
    participant WS1 as ⚡ WS Gateway 1
    participant Dispatcher as 🔀 Message Dispatcher
    participant DB as 💬 Cassandra Store
    participant Registry as ⚡ Session Registry
    participant WS2 as ⚡ WS Gateway 2
    actor Bob as 👤 Bob (Recipient)
    participant Offline as 📬 Offline Store
    participant Push as 🔔 Push Service

    Alice->>WS1: SendMessage(Recipient: Bob, Text: "Hey!", ClientMsgID: 104)
    WS1-->>Alice: Server Ack (Status: SENT, ServerMsgID: 991)
    WS1->>Dispatcher: RouteMessage(Bob, payload)

    Dispatcher->>DB: INSERT INTO messages (conv_id, msg_id, sender, text)
    Dispatcher->>Registry: Lookup(Bob)
    alt Bob is Online (Registered at WS Gateway 2)
        Registry-->>Dispatcher: Found: {Server: WS_Node2, Socket: s-881}
        Dispatcher->>WS2: ForwardMessage(Socket: s-881, payload)
        WS2->>Bob: Push Message over WebSocket
        Bob-->>WS2: Ack (DELIVERED)
        WS2->>WS1: Forward Delivery Ack
        WS1->>Alice: Update Checkmark: DELIVERED (✓✓)
    else Bob is Offline (No active session in Redis)
        Registry-->>Dispatcher: Not Found (Offline)
        Dispatcher->>Offline: Add to Bob's Pending Queue
        Dispatcher->>Push: Trigger Push Notification ("Alice: Hey!")
        Push->>Bob: Deliver FCM/APNs Wake-up Alert
    end

faqs.question: Why is Apache Cassandra preferred over PostgreSQL or MongoDB for chat history?
faqs.answer: Chat history exhibits a 99% sequential write-and-read pattern. Cassandra uses an LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge-tree) engine that appends writes sequentially to disk commit logs and in-memory Memtables, achieving hundreds of thousands of writes/sec without disk seek bottlenecks. Furthermore, data is partitioned by `conversation_id` with clustering key `message_id DESC`, making chat history pagination an instant range scan.

faqs.question: How do you handle 50 million concurrent WebSocket connections without running out of server memory?
faqs.answer: A single modern Linux server tuned with epoll can comfortably hold 500,000 to 1,000,000 idle TCP sockets if kernel buffers are tuned (`tcp_rmem`, `tcp_wmem` reduced to ~4KB per connection) and file descriptor limits (`ulimit -n`) are raised to 1M+. A fleet of 50-100 gateway servers easily manages 50M connections. Redis holds only `user_id -> server_ip` mapping (~64 bytes per user), consuming under 5GB of RAM.

faqs.question: How is message ordering guaranteed across mobile devices with clock drift?
faqs.answer: Never rely on client device clock timestamps. Use a monotonically increasing, centralized ID generator (Snowflake or ZooKeeper sequence generator) per conversation, or have the primary database assign an incrementing sequence number upon write. Messages are sorted and displayed exclusively by this server-assigned sequence ID.

faqs.question: How does Presence scale without overloading the system with millions of status broadcasts?
faqs.answer: Do not broadcast presence changes globally. Use a Pub/Sub subscription model: User A only subscribes to presence updates for users currently in their visible chat viewport or active contacts list (typically <50 people). For large group channels (e.g. 5,000 members), individual online indicators are disabled, and only an aggregate "1,420 Online" count is rendered.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Full-duplex WebSockets eliminate polling overhead, maintaining persistent connections for sub-100ms delivery
Session Registry (Redis) routes messages from any sending gateway node directly to the recipient's active server
Apache Cassandra (LSM-tree wide-column store) delivers high write throughput and fast range scans by conversation
Presence uses heartbeat leases and localized Pub/Sub subscriptions to prevent broadcast fan-out storms
Server-assigned Snowflake IDs guarantee strict chronological ordering unaffected by client device clock drift
data.takeaway: Real-time chat architectures achieve high responsiveness and scale by decoupling stateful WebSocket gateways from write-heavy NoSQL message storage, linked via an in-memory session registry.
